newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians, Chechens seek to clarify relations.
newsitem.headline: Russians, Chechens seek to clarify relations.

text.p: Russian officials and Chechen separatist delegates agreed on Tuesday to work out a provisional deal clarifying relations between Moscow and the breakaway region over the next few months, Interfax news agency said.

It quoted a Russian government official who took part in the meeting of a joint commission set up to monitor the latest peace deal in Chechnya as saying that a draft should be ready by Wednesday morning.

Government chief-of-staff Sergei Stepashin said that the deal would spell out relations between Moscow and Chechnya in the period to January 27, when the separatist administration plans elections for a regional leader and parliament.
Ivan Rybkin, the head of the Moscow delegation at the talks in the capital of the neighbouring region of Ingushetia, made clear that he expected the deal fairly soon.

Interfax quoted Rybkin, who succeeded Alexander Lebed as secretary of the Kremlin Security Council, as saying that Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and the head of the separatist government, Aslan Maskhadov, were expected to make "an important statement" in the near future.
Rybkin said that the contents of the deal would probably not be revealed for another day or two.

The peace deal, struck by Lebed and the rebels on August 31, ended 21 months of war which started when Moscow troops sent in troops to crush the region's independence drive. Tens of thousands of people, mainly civilians, died in the fighting.
Lebed was sacked last month by President Boris Yeltsin, accused of scheming to seize power.
The deal, under which Russian withdrew most of its troops from Chechnya, provided for a five-year deferral on the future political status of the region on the southern edge of the Russian Federation.
The rebels make little secret of the fact that they view the delay in decision-making as a face-saving excuse for Moscow to let Chechnya go.

But Moscow has ruled out granting Chechnya full independence and top Kremlin officials hope the five-year delay will be enough to change the situation so that Chechnya finds it more attractive to stay in Russia than to secede.
The controversy over the region's status has complicated post-war reconstruction of the region.

Some top Russian officials have suggested Moscow should invest in Chechen reconstruction only after receiving assurances that the region would remain part of the Russian Federation, something the rebels flatly reject.
Others say that if Russia does not help war-devastated Chechnya, anti-Russian sentiment will grow and the region will be even more reluctant to stay.

Following the withdrawal of Russian troops, the rebels have taken tight control of the region and scheduled local elections without consulting Moscow, adding to Kremlin suspicions that its funds invested in Chechnya could be spent in vain.
Rybkin, effectively admitting that Moscow could do little about the election, said it should conform with Russian legislation and foreign observers should be invited.
"The polls are Chechnya's internal affair and we have a strong enough legal basis to hold them," Movladi Udugov, a senior member of separatist government, replied bluntly.
